extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures for handling, editing, verifying, and disciplining manipulation of news photographs, including what edits are acceptable and how organizations should review and respond to altered images.

rubrics_metrics.name: No doctoring of pictures / zero tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: “Reuters has zero tolerance for any doctoring of pictures and constantly reminds its photographers, both staff and freelance, of this strict and unalterable policy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate manipulation of an image is described as the gravest breach of Reuters standards for photographers; discovery of such manipulation can result in termination of the relationship and removal of the photographer's images from the agency database (example: Reuters cut ties with Adnan Hajj and removed 920 pictures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial review requirement for sensitive regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reuters instituted tighter editing procedures for images from the Middle East, requiring that all such photos be reviewed by the top photo editors at Reuters’ global photo desk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher-risk conflict regions should have additional layers of editorial oversight to catch manipulation before distribution; implies centralized senior-editor review for sensitive geographic coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity verification and withdrawal of manipulated images
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulated images should be identified, withdrawn, and unaltered alternatives run when available (example: Reuters withdrew an altered image of smoke and later ran the unaltered image).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations should review suspect images, verify authenticity, remove doctored images from distribution/archives, and replace with unaltered versions when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted limited use of cloning tools
rubrics_metrics.description: “AP’s ethical guidelines permit use of ‘cloning’ in limited circumstances to clean up dirt or scratches from an image.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cloning (Photoshop's cloning tool) may be acceptable only to remove sensor dirt/glitches or scratches; it must not introduce or exaggerate scene elements (anti-pattern: using cloning in a way that creates extra smoke or flares).

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful and correct use of editing software
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors may result from careless use of software features (example: accidental double images, extra hands, or added flares due to misuse of cloning tools or other features).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographers must take care when editing to avoid producing artifacts that alter content; both the photographer and the editing desk share responsibility for catching such mistakes before transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational accountability and process oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: “There has to be an editing component that ensures the accuracy of the content… the overall process of the news organization that must be held accountable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond individual blame, news organizations should examine and strengthen workflows, editorial checks, and training to prevent manipulated images from being published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary review and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: When manipulation is discovered, organizations should review disciplinary actions against the photographer and other parties involved (examples: Reuters cut ties; AP reviewing actions; The Charlotte Observer terminated a photographer for altering photo colors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear consequences (termination, removal of images, internal review) serve both punitive and deterrent functions and should be part of policy for breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archive review after manipulation discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies reviewed historical submissions from implicated photographers to verify authenticity (example: AP reviewing all 193 of Hajj’s images in its archives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery of manipulation should trigger broader audits of a photographer’s archive to identify and remediate other possible altered images.
